If both debts have roughly an 18% interest rate, then reducing that to 12% would be great (if there were no other fees for the consolidation process).

If you have debts with very different interest rates, and the new rate you get after consolidation is the weighted average of the old ones, then consolidating probably increases the total amount of interest that you'll pay (consolidation can then still be a bit useful to make loans easier to manage, especially if you can consolidate multiple different loans into one).

Why you'll pay more interest? Imagine that you have a certain amount at an 18% interest rate and the same amount at a 6% interest rate, and they offer you a consolidation rate with a 12% interest rate. That's the weighted average, so that seems fair. But what that does is that you lose the ability to first focus on the amount at the 18% interest rate, and then be only left with a remaining balance at a much lower interest. Instead, you'll pay 12% during the whole duration of the pay-off process.

If you do not have any late payments or delinquent or defaulted debts, then your utilization rate currently is harming your credit score. This will improve quickly once you reduce your debt load. Your new debt load is reported within a month, and then the credit score also changes to reflect the new utilization rate (debts divided by total possible debt). So you should see an increase in your score within a few weeks, every time you improve that utilization rate.

Then your current high utilization rate is influencing your score significantly. That will improve soon after you start paying down your debts.

I would focus on one at a time. The one with the highest interest rate. Of course, in the meantime, pay the minimum required amount on all your other cards.

1. This is good for mathematical reasons, because paying down the card with the highest interest rate first will mean that you start paying less interest the soonest, and paying less interest means that you can pay down the principal quicker. So the paying down process goes faster. (You can try an online tool with your situation and toggle between "snowball" and "avalanche" methods to see how much the difference is for you).

2. It is also good for psychological reasons. Some scientific studies have found that people made *more* progress if they focused their efforts on one specific card. They simply put more money towards the cards because they continued to be more motivated. So I think that could help you as well, to stay motivated.

I think it's really good that you've set yourself this goal. It is probably a big motivation to think that you'll become debt-free in just one year's time.

A few other things you could do to stay motivated:

1. Track your progress. Make a chart of how much you owe and watch it go down over time. Or make a list of the cards that you still owe on, and put a big strike through one when you're done with it. Or make a sheet with one circle for every $10 or $100 that you owe, and color it in when you've paid it. Whatever method works for you (some people love graphs, other people love pictures, etc).
2. Also celebrate the milestones: the first $100 paid down, every hundred that you get closer to $0, et cetera. Of course, don't celebrate by spending a lot of money, but reward yourself for actually doing it.
3. Keep a note or visual cue in your wallet and perhaps next to your computer screen that will remind you not to spend money if you don't need to. Could be a sticker, a piece of paper, a picture, a word...
